screens.title: Triggering Workflows: The 'on' Event
screens.narratorSegment: The 'on' keyword in your GitHub Actions workflow file is crucial because it defines the events that will trigger your automation. Without a correctly configured 'on' section, your workflow simply won't run. Imagine you're building a continuous integration pipeline; you'd want it to kick off every time new code is pushed to your main development branch. This is where the 'push' event comes in, allowing you to specify branches like 'main' or 'develop'. Similarly, for code reviews, the 'pull_request' event ensures your CI checks run automatically when a pull request is opened or updated. Beyond these common triggers, 'workflow_dispatch' provides a way to manually trigger workflows from the GitHub UI, which is great for ad-hoc tasks or deployments. You can even use 'schedule' with cron syntax to run workflows at specific times, perhaps for nightly builds or cleanup tasks. Furthermore, you can refine these triggers using 'paths' to only run the workflow when changes occur in specific directories, preventing unnecessary runs and saving resources. Understanding these event types is fundamental to designing efficient and responsive CI pipelines. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 4›Workflow Triggers

Triggering Workflows: The 'on' Event

The on keyword defines the events that trigger your GitHub Actions workflow, dictating when your automation should run.

Push

Triggers on code pushes to specified branches (e.g., main, develop).

Pull Request

Runs when a PR is opened, synchronized, or reopened for target branches.

Schedule

Executes at specified times using cron syntax (e.g., daily builds).

Workflow Dispatch

Allows manual triggering of the workflow from the GitHub UI.

Paths Filtering

Filter triggers to run only when changes occur in specific directories.

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
  workflow_dispatch:
Key Takeaway

Careful configuration of the on event ensures your workflows run precisely when and how you intend, optimizing resource usage and CI efficiency.

screens.title: Jobs and Runners: Where Your Code Runs
screens.narratorSegment: Once a workflow is triggered, it executes one or more 'jobs'. Think of a job as a distinct unit of work, like building your application or running tests. By default, these jobs run in parallel, which can significantly speed up your CI process. However, you can also configure dependencies, ensuring one job completes successfully before another begins. Each job runs on a fresh instance of a 'runner', which is essentially the server that executes your workflow steps. GitHub offers two main types of runners. First, we have GitHub-hosted runners, which are virtual machines provided and managed by GitHub. These are pre-installed with common software and are automatically scaled, making them incredibly convenient for most projects. Examples include 'ubuntu-latest' or 'windows-latest'. Second, there are self-hosted runners, which are machines you set up and manage yourself. These are ideal when you have specific hardware requirements, need custom software installations, or require access to private network resources that GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach. Choosing between these depends on your project's unique needs for control, cost, and environment customization. keyIdea.text: Jobs are independent units of work that execute on runners, which can be GitHub-managed or self-managed, depending on project needs.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 4›Jobs & Runners

Jobs and Runners: Where Your Code Runs

A workflow run is made up of one or more jobs, each executing on a dedicated runner environment.

GitHub-hosted Runners

Virtual machines provided and managed by GitHub. They come pre-installed with common software and are automatically scaled.

  • •Convenient and easy to use, no infrastructure management.
  • •Examples: ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest.
  • •Limited customization for specific hardware or software.
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

Self-hosted Runners

Machines you set up and manage yourself. They offer greater control over the environment.

  • •Useful for specific hardware, custom software, or private network access.
  • •Full control over the operating system and installed tools.
  • •Requires manual setup, maintenance, and scaling.
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: self-hosted
Key Takeaway

Selecting the appropriate runner type is crucial for balancing convenience, cost, and environmental control in your CI/CD workflows.

screens.title: Defining Tasks: 'uses' vs. 'run'
screens.narratorSegment: Within each job, 'steps' are the individual tasks that get executed. GitHub Actions provides two primary ways to define these steps: using 'uses' for pre-built actions, and 'run' for executing shell commands. The 'uses' keyword allows you to leverage existing GitHub Actions, which are reusable pieces of code designed to perform specific tasks. These can come from the GitHub Marketplace, like 'actions/checkout@v4' to get your repository code, or 'actions/setup-node@v4' to configure a Node. js environment. Using these actions saves you time and effort, as you don't have to write the underlying logic yourself. They promote reusability and consistency across workflows. On the other hand, the 'run' keyword lets you execute arbitrary shell commands directly on the runner. This provides immense flexibility for tasks that don't have a dedicated action, such as installing dependencies with 'npm install' or running custom scripts. You can chain multiple commands using multi-line YAML syntax. The choice between 'uses' and 'run' often comes down to whether a suitable pre-built action exists for your task or if you need to execute custom logic specific to your project.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 4›Steps: Uses vs Run

Defining Tasks: 'uses' vs. 'run'

Steps are individual tasks within a job, executed either by reusable actions or direct shell commands.

uses: GitHub Actions

Executes a reusable GitHub Action, often from the Marketplace. Promotes consistency and saves development time.

  • •Pre-built, tested, and maintained by the community or GitHub.
  • •Examples: actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-node@v4.
  • •Requires trusting external code; always pin to specific versions.
- name: Checkout Repository
  uses: actions/checkout@v4

run: Shell Commands

Executes shell commands directly on the runner. Offers maximum flexibility for custom logic.

  • •Ideal for installing dependencies, running scripts, or custom build commands.
  • •Can be multi-line for complex sequences of commands.
  • •Requires the runner environment to have the necessary tools installed.
- name: Install Dependencies
  run: npm ci
Key Takeaway

Combine uses for standardized tasks and run for custom operations to build comprehensive and efficient workflow steps.

screens.title: Building CI: Workflow Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical example of a GitHub Actions workflow for a Node. js application, starting with the foundational setup. Every workflow begins with a 'name', which is a human-readable label displayed in the GitHub UI, making it easy to identify your pipeline. Next, the 'on' section defines when this workflow should run. In our example, we're triggering it on 'push' events to both the 'main' and 'develop' branches, and also on 'pull_request' events targeting these same branches. This ensures that every code change and every proposed merge gets automatically checked. The workflow then defines 'jobs', which are the high-level tasks. Here, we have a single 'build' job. The 'runs-on' keyword specifies the runner environment, and we're using 'ubuntu-latest', a GitHub-hosted runner, for convenience and broad compatibility. The first step within our job uses 'actions/checkout@v4' to fetch your repository's code onto the runner, which is essential for any subsequent operations. Following this, 'actions/setup-node@v4' configures the Node. js environment, specifying version 18. x and enabling npm dependency caching for faster, more efficient builds. This initial setup lays the groundwork for all subsequent build and test operations.

keyIdea.title: Foundation for a Robust CI Pipeline
keyIdea.text: A well-defined workflow name, precise triggers, and proper environment setup are crucial for any CI pipeline.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 4›Workflow Setup
# .github/workflows/node-ci.yml
name: Node.js CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, develop ] # Trigger on pushes
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main, develop ] # Trigger on PRs

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest # GitHub-hosted runner

    steps:
    - name: Checkout Repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4 # Get code

    - name: Use Node.js 18.x
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4 # Setup Node.js
      with:
        node-version: '18.x'
        cache: 'npm' # Cache npm dependencies

Building CI: Workflow Setup

This initial section defines the workflow's identity, triggers, and the environment where it will run, along with essential setup steps.

Workflow Identity & Triggers

The name provides a clear label, while on specifies events like push and pull_request to initiate the workflow.

Job Definition & Runner

A build job is defined to run on ubuntu-latest, a GitHub-hosted virtual machine, providing a consistent execution environment.

Code Checkout & Environment Setup

actions/checkout@v4 retrieves the repository code, and actions/setup-node@v4 configures the Node.js environment with dependency caching.

Key Takeaway

A robust CI workflow starts with clear identification, precise triggers, and a well-prepared execution environment to ensure reliable and efficient builds.

screens.title: Building CI: Dependencies & Tests
screens.narratorSegment: Continuing our Node. js CI workflow, the next critical steps involve managing dependencies and ensuring code quality through linting and testing. After setting up the Node. js environment, we use the 'npm ci' command to install project dependencies. It's important to note that 'npm ci' is preferred over 'npm install' in CI environments because it performs a clean installation based strictly on the 'package-lock. json' file. This guarantees that you're always using the exact same dependency versions, preventing unexpected build failures due to package updates. Next, we include a step to run linting, assuming you have a 'lint' script defined in your 'package. json'. Linting is vital for maintaining code style, catching potential errors early, and ensuring consistency across your codebase. Finally, the workflow executes unit tests using 'npm test'. We've added flags to generate a coverage report and output test results to a JSON file. Running tests automatically on every change is the cornerstone of continuous integration, providing immediate feedback on the health and correctness of your application. These steps collectively ensure that your code is not only buildable but also adheres to quality standards and functions as expected.

screens.title: GitHub Actions vs. Azure Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: When it comes to CI/CD, both GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines are powerful, enterprise-grade solutions, but they each have distinct strengths. screens.title: Securing & Optimizing Your Workflows
screens.narratorSegment: To build truly robust and secure GitHub Actions workflows, it's crucial to be aware of common mistakes and follow best practices. One frequent pitfall is incorrect 'on' event configuration, leading to workflows not triggering as expected. Always double-check branch names and event types. Another common error is forgetting to use 'actions/checkout@v4', which means your repository code won't be available on the runner, causing subsequent steps to fail. Dependency caching issues can also arise; while actions like 'setup-node' offer caching, incorrect cache keys or paths can lead to cache misses or stale caches, slowing down your builds. For security, never hardcode sensitive information like A P I keys directly in your workflow file. Instead, use GitHub Secrets, which are encrypted environment variables securely stored in your repository settings. Access them via 'secrets. MY_SECRET_NAME'. Also, be mindful of the default 'GITHUB_TOKEN' permissions; if your workflow needs to perform actions like creating releases, you might need to explicitly grant additional permissions. Finally, when using Marketplace actions, always verify their source and reputation, and pin to specific versions like '@v4' to prevent unexpected changes. Adhering to these practices will significantly enhance the reliability and security of your CI pipelines.

Module 3›Chapter 4›Best Practices

Securing & Optimizing Your Workflows

Avoid common pitfalls and implement best practices to ensure your GitHub Actions workflows are reliable, efficient, and secure.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Incorrect on Event Config

Workflows may not trigger if branch names or event types are misconfigured. Always verify your on section.

Missing actions/checkout

Forgetting to checkout your repository means your code won't be available for subsequent build or test steps.

Dependency Caching Issues

Incorrect cache keys or paths can lead to cache misses or stale caches, impacting build performance.

Security & Trust Best Practices

Secrets Management

Never hardcode sensitive info. Use GitHub Secrets, accessed via secrets.MY_SECRET_NAME, for encrypted environment variables.

Marketplace Action Trust

Verify sources and reputations of Marketplace actions. Always use specific versions (e.g., @v4) to prevent unexpected changes.

GITHUB_TOKEN Permissions

Understand and explicitly grant necessary permissions for the default GITHUB_TOKEN if your workflow needs to interact with the GitHub API beyond default scope.

Key Takeaway

Proactive attention to workflow configuration, security best practices, and action vetting is paramount for building reliable and secure CI/CD pipelines.

Adhering to these practices will significantly enhance the reliability and security of your CI pipelines.

Continuing our review of key concepts, let's look at the operational components of a workflow. A 'Job' is a set of steps that executes on a single runner, typically in parallel with other jobs in a workflow. It's the logical grouping of tasks. Within each job, a 'Step' is an individual task, which can either be a shell command using 'run' or a reusable GitHub Action using 'uses'. Steps are the granular instructions that make up your automation. Finally, the 'Runner' is the server that runs your workflow. We learned about both GitHub-hosted runners, which are managed by GitHub, and self-hosted runners, which you manage yourself for greater control. These components work together to execute your automated processes, from fetching code to running tests and deploying applications.
